The 14-day sampling window was adequate to define the absorption phase for a monoclonal antibody administered s.c., while acknowledging that sparse late terminal data limited definitive estimation of terminal half-life and total exposure.

Absorption following 8 mg/kg s.c. administration in Cynomolgus monkeys was consistent with a delayed rise to measurable plasma concentrations, compatible with lymphatic uptake expected for IgG1 monoclonal antibodies. Peak concentrations were observed within the 14-day sampling horizon, indicating completion of the primary absorption phase in most animals; the study duration did not allow full characterization of the terminal elimination phase. No formulation-related differences in qualitative absorption behavior were apparent between the two AVT02 lots within the constraints of the small group sizes and exploratory design.

Distribution was expected to be restricted to the vascular and interstitial compartments typical of IgG1, mediated by FcRn recycling; no dedicated tissue distribution studies were performed, which is aligned with ICH M3(R2) expectations for biotechnology-derived products in early clinical development when supported by platform knowledge. The observed plasma concentration-time profiles over 14 days were consistent with limited extravascular distribution and ongoing FcRn-mediated protection from catabolism.

Metabolism of adalimumab-class antibodies proceeds via proteolytic catabolism to peptides and amino acids without identified cytochrome P450–mediated pathways; no specific metabolite profiling was performed. This is consistent with established monoclonal antibody disposition mechanisms and acceptable for Phase 1 initiation under ICH M3(R2), with risk management focused on immunogenicity rather than small-molecule metabolic interactions.

Overall, the nonclinical PK dataset is appropriate for a Phase 1 entry for a biosimilar monoclonal antibody, consistent with ICH M3(R2) expectations, while recognizing that formal comparative PK will be addressed in clinical studies and that PBPK applications must meet EMA qualification standards.
